# UKIP 2010 Manifesto Summary

The UK Independence Party's 2010 manifesto centres on one overarching principle: Britain must withdraw from the European Union to reclaim its sovereignty, prosperity, and national identity. UKIP positions itself as the authentic voice of the British majority, citing polls showing over half the population wanting EU withdrawal whilst being denied any referendum by the "LibLabConsensus."

## Core Argument: Freedom Through Withdrawal

UKIP identifies three essential freedoms that EU membership denies Britain. **Freedom of Action** would allow the UK to negotiate its own trade deals and control its destiny rather than holding merely 9% of EU votes. **Freedom of Resources** would save £6.4 billion annually in net contributions, plus escape regulations costing up to £120 billion yearly. **Freedom of the People** would restore democratic governance from Westminster rather than "unelected bureaucrats, commissioners, multiple presidents and judges."

## Economic Vision

The party proposes radical tax simplification: a 31% flat tax replacing income tax bands and National Insurance, whilst raising the threshold to £11,500 to remove minimum-wage earners from taxation entirely. Inheritance tax would be abolished. The manifesto commits to substantial public sector reduction, aiming to return government to its 1997 size by eliminating "quangos and non-jobs."

UKIP champions manufacturing revival through five major programmes: enhanced defence equipment spending, nuclear power station construction, flood defences, transport infrastructure, and prison building—all structured to benefit British-based firms and create one million skilled jobs.

## Immigration and Identity

Describing mass immigration as a "deliberate attempt to water down the British identity," UKIP proposes an immediate five-year freeze on permanent settlement immigration, aspiring to cap future immigration at 50,000 annually. Only EU withdrawal enables genuine border control, the party argues. Illegal immigrants would face mandatory deportation with "no question of an amnesty."

The manifesto explicitly opposes multiculturalism, instead promoting "uniculturalism"—a single British culture embracing all backgrounds. This includes teaching Britain's positive global contributions, safeguarding imperial measurements, and creating a Commonwealth Day holiday.

## Defence and Foreign Policy

Armed forces spending would increase by 40%, expanding the Army by 25% and restoring the Royal Navy. UKIP commits to maintaining independent nuclear deterrence and strengthening NATO whilst withdrawing from EU military operations.

The Commonwealth receives particular emphasis as Britain's natural trading partners—50 nations sharing language, legal systems, and democratic values. UKIP would pursue a Commonwealth Free Trade Area potentially covering 20% of international trade.

## Public Services

The NHS would remain free at point of delivery but face structural reform through elected County Health Boards, franchising services to private and charitable providers, and replacing bureaucrats with clinical leadership. Education would see "School Vouchers" enabling parental choice between state, private, and faith schools, alongside restored grammar schools and new "professional schools."

Pensions would be simplified into a non-means-tested Citizen's Pension of £130 weekly, whilst unfunded public sector pensions would be frozen.

## Democratic Reform

UKIP proposes "Direct Democracy" allowing 5% of voters to trigger binding referenda. Electoral reform through Alternative Vote Plus would ensure MPs earn majority support. Regional government would be abolished, with county councils becoming the prime local unit. Directly elected boards would oversee police, education, and health services.

## Environment and Energy

Taking a sceptical stance on man-made climate change, UKIP would repeal the Climate Change Act, halt renewable subsidies, and invest in nuclear power to provide 50% of electricity needs. The party explicitly rejects "global warming propaganda" in schools.

Throughout, the manifesto presents EU withdrawal not as isolationism but as liberation—enabling Britain to pursue its global destiny as the world's sixth-largest economy, Commonwealth leader, and UN Security Council member, free from Brussels constraints.
